match.reason: None of the bank points teaches that a polynomial of degree n has at most n real solutions. The closest, the cubic graphs card, covers factorising and sketching cubics but not that bound or the numerical method, and the graph-intersection card is about two functions meeting rather than polynomial degree.

draft.title: Polynomial equations
card: A polynomial of degree n has at most n real solutions. A cubic has at most 3, and a quadratic at most 2. It can have fewer.
To solve by factorising, move every term to one side so the other side is 0. Factorise, then set each factor equal to 0 (the null factor law).
Example: x³ − 4x = 0 gives x(x − 2)(x + 2) = 0, so x = 0, x = 2 or x = −2. Three solutions from a cubic.
If it will not factorise, graph y = the polynomial. The real solutions are the x-intercepts. A calculator can also find them numerically.
draft.remember: Set one side to 0, then factorise. A degree n polynomial has at most n real solutions.

a.q: How many real solutions does x³ − 9x = 0 have?
a.why: x³ − 9x = x(x − 3)(x + 3) = 0, so x = 0, 3 or −3. Three solutions is the most a cubic can have. Dividing both sides by x would lose x = 0 and leave only 2.
a.clue: Factorise fully, then set each factor to 0.

b.q: What are all the real solutions of x³ = 4x²?
b.why: Move terms to one side: x³ − 4x² = 0, so x²(x − 4) = 0. Then x = 0 or x = 4. Dividing both sides by x² would lose x = 0, which is the tempting mistake that gives x = 4 only.
b.clue: Get 0 on one side before you factorise.

final.title: Polynomial equations
card: A polynomial of degree \(n\) has at most \(n\) real solutions. A cubic has at most 3, and a quadratic at most 2. It can have fewer.
To solve by factorising, move every term to one side so the other side is 0. Factorise, then set each factor equal to 0 (the null factor law).
Example: \(x^{3} - 4x = 0\) gives \(x(x - 2)(x + 2) = 0\), so \(x = 0\), \(x = 2\) or \(x = -2\). Three solutions from a cubic.
If it will not factorise, graph \(y = P(x)\), where \(P(x)\) is the polynomial. The real solutions are the x-intercepts. A calculator can also find them numerically.
final.remember: Set one side to 0, then factorise. A degree \(n\) polynomial has at most \(n\) real solutions.

a.q: How many real solutions does \(x^{3} - 9x = 0\) have?
a.why: \(x^{3} - 9x = x(x - 3)(x + 3) = 0\), so \(x = 0\), 3 or \(-3\). Three solutions is the most a cubic can have. Dividing both sides by \(x\) would lose \(x = 0\) and leave only 2.
a.clue: Factorise fully, then set each factor to 0.

b.q: What are all the real solutions of \(x^{3} = 4x^{2}\)?
b.why: Move terms to one side: \(x^{3} - 4x^{2} = 0\), so \(x^{2}(x - 4) = 0\). Then \(x = 0\) or \(x = 4\). Dividing both sides by \(x^{2}\) would lose \(x = 0\), which is the tempting mistake that gives \(x = 4\) only.
b.clue: Get 0 on one side before you factorise.
